title: The mist cleared
hookLine: the true Guru Nanak appeared, the mist cleared and light spread through the world (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1.27)

cards: A winter morning on a country road. Fog so thick the headlights reach the next post and stop. Everything is gray: the fields, the trees, the road itself.
You drive slowly, guessing. Then, without anyone deciding it, the sun gets high enough.
The fog thins, lifts, and is simply gone, and the whole road is there, the fields on either side, a farmhouse you didn't know was close. Nothing new was added. It was all there already.

teach.h: THE SUN RISES, THE STARS HIDE.
teach.b: A few stanzas on in his first var, Bhai Gurdas reaches for big pictures. The true Guru Nanak appeared, he says.

teach.h: NOT A NEW WORLD: THE MIST CLEARED.
teach.b: The mist cleared, and there was light in the world. It was like the sun coming up: the stars hide and the darkness runs off. And like a lion's roar, at which the herd of deer scatters and can't hold its ground.
Notice what kind of picture this is. Bhai Gurdas doesn't say Nanak built a new world. He says the mist cleared.
A sunrise doesn't create the road, the fields or the farmhouse. It shows what was already standing there. In Sikh teaching, the One was never absent from the world.
What had gone missing was the seeing. Then Bhai Gurdas says what that light looked like on the ground, and it's surprisingly homely. Wherever Baba set his foot, a place of worship grew up.

teach.h: A DHARAMSAL IN HOUSE AFTER HOUSE.
teach.b: In house after house there was a dharamsal, a place for the sangat to gather, with kirtan sung, and it felt like a festival every day.
That's how he measures the light: not in thunder, but in ordinary homes where people started to gather, sit together and sing.
It fits what you learned in year two. The daily banis are that kind of light: small, repeated, kept in houses. A dawn that comes again tomorrow.

how: In the gurdwara, this stanza of Bhai Gurdas's first var may be sung as kirtan or explained in katha, as a picture of Guru Nanak's coming.

o: a monastery where renunciants live apart
a court where religious law is judged
a place where the sangat gathers to sing

games.q: inside the stanza — tap the pairs.

s: Bhai Gurdas says Nanak made a brand new world
he says the mist cleared: the light shows what was already there.
the light shows up in ordinary homes, gathering and singing
a dharamsal in house after house, kirtan like a festival.

games.q: you're telling the story, and the Guru has just arrived. how do you show the light on the ground?
o: people gathering in homes to sing together.
a single sign in the sky, and nothing after.
games.why: Bhai Gurdas measures it in homes: a place of worship in house after house, and kirtan, like a festival every day.

practice: Open a curtain or a blind all the way, even if it's already light, even if there's only a streetlamp, and sit facing it.

Let your eyes rest on what was already there, a wall, a tree, a rooftop, the sky: nothing new added to the room, only let in to be seen. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly as the light comes in.

wordCard.voice: Dharamsal, a place where the sangat gathered to sing, springing up wherever Guru Nanak set foot, with kirtan and a festival feeling every day.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: light. In the stanza, the mist clears and there is light in the world.

carryVoice: Your line: it was all there already. The mist clears; the road was never missing. Seven hundred days, and counting.

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 27 (satgur Nanak pragtiaa, mitti dhundh jag chaanan hoaa)
